rv.q: TUTA Theatre's Crime and Punishment is an intense and gripping production that fully captures the emotional and philosophical weight of Dostoevsky's novel.
As Rasolnikov, Clifton Frei is nigh perfect.

This “Crime and Punishment” has a mesmerizing power, not only because of its psychological tension, nail-biting game of wits, and suspenseful plot, but because its guiding idea focuses on how true moral redemption and peace cannot be achieved through cold rationality alone.
Guilt, generosity, despair, and ultimately the need to dig through the dirt and find reasons to keep going recur in this entrancing show.
The TUTA Theatre (The Utopian Theatre Asylum) really proves that good things really do come in small packages.
Most unsettling of all was the creeping sensation, as the story unfolds, that nearly everything the audience witnesses could happen, even is happening, today.
It might be a crime not to check out this nimble adaptation of the literary classic.

The play doesn’t focus on the crime, or the human punishment to come. It is a psychological piece, incorporating Dostoevsky’s obsessions with the terrible poverty of the people of Russia, with man’s inhumanity to man, and to the ultimate necessity of charity and hope of redemption through God.

cn.t: TUTA Theatre's intimate adaptation transforms Dostoevsky's sprawling novel into a gripping psychological thriller. Critics praise the visually striking, chilling production that captures the guilt and suspense of the classic tale.
